subject: programmatically creating a Data Frame for Java

messages.author: 892966d513e3f9d4
messages.subject: programmatically creating a Data Frame for Java
parts:
Hi,

I would like to programmatically create a Data Frame in Java, and expose it into a renjin session.

Since the documentation says that data frames are basically vectors, I tried to build a vector using Vector.NamedBuilder, but the resulting entity does not work as data frame.

How can I build a data frame from Java? What is a data frame layout in term of primitives? (since to my understanding, data frame is not a real primitive).

thanks in advance for your help,

best,
Francesco

messages.subject: Re: programmatically creating a Data Frame for Java
parts:
Thanks Parham,

that solved my issue.
I was missing the fact that I need to set the "class".

After that, I discovered (it is not covered by the example) that the attribute "row.names" is also supposed to be set.

I think a good solution is something like:

 dataFrame.setAttribute(Symbols.ROW_NAMES, new IntSequence(1, 1, length))

Maybe it would be a good idea to give prominence to these facts in the interoperability documentation.

thanks,
Francesco

messages.author: 3b104dc6686d0c85
messages.subject: Re: programmatically creating a Data Frame for Java
parts:
Dear Francesco,

if you think that the documentation can be improved, you can open an issue at https://github.com/bedatadriven/renjin-docs/issues. Of course, you can also improve the docs yourself and send us a pull request which we welcome very much!

One remark regarding your first message: a data frame is indeed a compound data type in R and it's essentially a list with special characteristics:
  1. each element has the same length,
  2. the class attribute includes the string "data.frame", and
  3. the attribute row.names exists and is a character or integer vector with length equal to the length of each list element.
So in Renjin you build a (named) list and add the required attributes, which is very much like doing the following in R:

structure(list(a=1, b=2), class = "data.frame", row.names = 1L)

If you don't set the row.names attribute, you will get what looks like a data frame with zero rows but the columns do have:

> structure(list(a=1, b=2), class = "data.frame") -> x
> x
[1] a b
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
> str(x)
'data.frame': 0 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ a: num 1
 $ b: num 2

So, indeed, it is required to correctly set the row.names attribute to get a true data frame.

​Regards,

Maarten-Jan
